activities.anchor: Two opposing hormones, one defended band
activities.caption: pair each player with its move in the loop
activities.name: nurLoopMatch

config.prompt: The glucose loop and its failure modes — pair them:

pairs.right: moves glucose into cells and storage when it rises
releases stored glucose back when it falls
loses the tissue's response to insulin

config.why: Each disease of the loop reads as a failure mode — which is why vital signs are controllers' outputs, not random biological noise.

activities.anchor: the raw numbers lie while the body spends its reserves
activities.caption: true or false — reading the dashboard
activities.name: nurNormalJudge

statements.s: Normal raw numbers always mean a stable patient.
statements.why: Compensation can hold the gauges at normal while the patient worsens — a young adult can defend blood pressure while quietly draining reserves.

statements.s: Trends and ratios reveal what isolated digits hide.
statements.why: The professional habit — and exactly what the derived indices are for.

statements.s: A racing pulse can be a controller working hard, not a malfunction.
statements.why: Once vital signs are seen as controllers' outputs, patterns acquire explanations.

statements.s: Derived indices exist to decorate the chart.
statements.why: They move first — that is their entire clinical value.

activities.anchor: which is the difference between watching a patient and assessing one
activities.caption: file each signature under its condition
activities.name: nurSignsSort

config.prompt: Three conditions, one dashboard — file each finding:

items.label: a pump failing to match demand — breathlessness, oedema, crackles
fluid backed into lungs and legs
infection escalating to body-wide inflammation and circulatory failure
rising heart and respiratory rates with falling pressure and confusion

config.why: The science converts 'the patient looks unwell' into a specific, testable, escalating hypothesis — that is the licence's judgement at work.

activities.anchor: applied microbiology with a logic you can derive from first principles
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the chain of infection
activities.name: nurChainCloze

config.text: Every infection needs the chain: a %%0%%, a reservoir, a portal of exit, a mode of %%1%%, a portal of entry, and a %%2%% host. Break any link and transmission stops.
config.hint: The six links — the playbook aims at the one humans control.

activities.anchor: so the corridor does not become the next reservoir
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the three armours
activities.name: nurRouteSpot

config.prompt: One line of this precautions note is wrong — click it:
lines: Contact spread (C. difficile, MRSA) is broken by gloves, gowns and meticulous hand hygiene.
Droplet spread travels in wet projectiles about a metre — blocked by a surgical mask and spacing.
Airborne spread rides drying nuclei that hang in the air for hours.
Airborne precautions call for a surgical mask and an open window; the N95 is optional extra credit.
Same hands, three different sciences, three different protections.
config.correction: Airborne spread (tuberculosis, measles) demands the respirator-grade N95 and a negative-pressure room — wet-projectile defences do nothing against nuclei that hang in air for hours.
config.why: The armour comes from the route — the ritual is wrong until you know the microbe.

activities.caption: drag across the drug's two sciences
activities.name: nurAdmeCompare

config.prompt: Drag across the two symmetrical sciences of every drug:

before.label: what the body does to the drug
before.text: Pharmacokinetics: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion — the dose's journey and how much of it survives the trip.

after.label: what the drug does to the body
after.text: Pharmacodynamics: which receptors are touched, whether they are turned up or down, and how that maps to effect.

config.why: The order says what to give; the bedside check is that, for this body, at this moment, by this route, the dose lands inside the therapeutic window — not below it (useless) or above it (harm).

activities.anchor: a patient cannot "feel" a new antidepressant on day two
activities.caption: guess the magnitude — the 24-hour leftover
activities.name: nurHalfLifeEstimate

config.prompt: A drug with a 4-hour half-life: 500 mg taken now. Roughly how much remains after 24 hours?
config.why: Halve every 4 hours: 250, 125, 62, 31, 16, 8 — and read forward, four to five half-lives is the steady-state clock for regular dosing.
config.context: the same curve, read forward, is why dosing discipline follows the half-life

activities.anchor: It is the most human error in pharmacology
activities.caption: walk the day-four phone call
activities.name: nurStopBranch

config.root: Day four of an antibiotic course, the patient calls: 'I feel completely better — why finish it?' Walk the answer.

start.text: What have the symptoms actually reported?

choices.label: That the infection is fully cleared
That the drug has knocked the population down — the hardiest cells survive

wrong.text: Not quite: symptoms are what the patient notices, and they resolve before the underlying process does.

survivors.text: Stopping now selectively breeds resistance — the survivors are the hardiest. And for blood-pressure or antidepressant medication, the drug controls a chronic condition rather than curing it, so symptoms return when the level falls.

choices.label: So who sets the stop date?

done.text: Honest stop dates are a stewardship skill: the science sets the end, not the symptom.

config.why: Microbiology and pharmacology conspire here — the mechanism, not the feeling, decides the stop date.
